204.title: Legion (Mark 5:1–20)
204.hook: a man living in tombs is freed and asks to follow; go home and tell your friends
204.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of the Gerasene man in the weekday Mass readings; the Church's rite of exorcism is reserved to a priest with the bishop's permission and requires that medical and psychological causes be ruled out first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peace, be still, and a calmed sea. Your line was who is this. Today, the boat lands on the other side, and we find out what the storm was crossing toward. Day two hundred four.

The boat scrapes onto a beach on the far side of the lake. This is foreign country, Gentile land. There are pigs on the hillside, which tells you no observant Jewish family farms here. And before Jesus is even out of the boat, a man comes running at him from the graveyard. He lives there, among the tombs. People have tried to chain him, and he's snapped the chains. Day and night he's out in the hills, crying out and cutting himself with stones. Nobody can hold him. Nobody goes near. Today: Legion.
screen: `THE FAR SIDE OF THE LAKE.` → `A MAN AMONG THE TOMBS.` → `NO CHAIN CAN HOLD HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Jesus asks him, what is thy name? And the answer comes, in the Douay-Rheims: "My name is Legion, for we are many." A legion was a Roman army unit of thousands of soldiers, the most feared force in the world. So the name says: I'm not one person anymore. I'm occupied. Many scholars notice that the word would have made listeners think of Rome's own legions, occupying the land. Second, the pigs. The spirits beg to be sent into a great herd of swine, about two thousand, Mark says, and the herd rushes down the steep bank into the sea. It's a strange scene, and people have puzzled over it for centuries. The gospel doesn't explain it. Third, the town. The herdsmen run and tell everyone. People come out and find the man sitting there, clothed, in his right mind. And they're afraid. Not of the storm or the demons now, of Jesus. They beg him to leave. Fourth, the surprise. As Jesus gets into the boat, the healed man begs to go with him. Of course he does. You'd expect Jesus to say yes; he's been calling followers all along. He says no. "Go into thy house to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had mercy on thee." So the man becomes the first messenger to the Gentiles in Mark's gospel. He goes around the ten towns of the Decapolis telling what happened, and everyone marvels. One note of care: the gospel speaks of unclean spirits. Catholics don't read it as saying that mental illness is demonic; the Church asks that illness be treated by medicine.
screen: `MY NAME IS LEGION.` · `TWO THOUSAND SWINE INTO THE SEA.` · `THE TOWN BEGS HIM TO LEAVE.` · `NOT FOLLOW. GO HOME AND TELL.` · then, large: `TELL THEM HOW GREAT THINGS THE LORD HATH DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell someone what's been good. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last month for one thing that went right. Something healed, a worry that lifted, a kindness you didn't expect, a way you've changed. Let it come into focus. Now think of one person at home, or a friend, who'd be glad to hear it. If you pray, give thanks for it first. Then decide when you'll tell them, today. The bell holds the time.
Legion. The name the tormented man gives, for we are many: a word borrowed from the Roman army. He's freed, and sent home to tell. Today's word.
Your line: go home and tell. Today, tell one person close to you about something good that's happened, without making it a sermon. Just tell it. Day two hundred four.

205.title: The story inside the story (Mark 5:21–43)
205.hook: Mark sandwiches the bleeding woman inside Jairus's daughter; both are daughters
205.howItsDone: Catholics hear the raising of Jairus's daughter and the healing of the woman at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time (Year B), and the Church prays for the sick through the sacrament of anointing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Legion: a man freed and sent home. Your line was go home and tell. Who did you tell something good? Today Jesus crosses back, and Mark tells two stories at once. Day two hundred five.

You're rushing to the hospital. Someone you love is in trouble, and every minute counts. And then, in the hallway, someone stops you. Excuse me. Can I ask you something? Everything in you says: not now. That's the knot at the center of today's reading. Mark does something clever here. He starts one story, stops it halfway, tells a whole second story in the middle, and only then finishes the first. Scholars call it a Markan sandwich. And the two stories turn out to be mirrors of each other. Today: the story inside the story.
screen: `RUSHING TO THE HOSPITAL.` → `SOMEONE STOPS YOU.` → `A MARKAN SANDWICH.`

segments.voice: First, the outside story. Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, an important man, falls at Jesus's feet. My little daughter is dying, he says. Come and lay your hands on her. Jesus goes, and the crowd presses in around him. Second, the inside story. In that crowd is a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years. She's spent everything on doctors and only got worse. Under the law, the bleeding also kept her ritually unclean, cut off. She thinks: if I can just touch his clothes. She does, and she feels it: she's healed. And Jesus stops. "Who hath touched my garments?" The disciples almost laugh: the whole crowd is touching you. Meanwhile Jairus is standing there. His daughter is dying. Jesus waits. The woman comes forward, trembling, and tells him the whole truth. And he says: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace." Third, the bad news. While he's still speaking, messengers arrive. Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the master any further? Jesus turns to Jairus: "Fear not, only believe." He goes to the house, takes the girl by the hand, and says in Aramaic: talitha cumi, little girl, arise. She gets up and walks. And Jesus tells them, give her something to eat. Fourth, the mirrors. The woman has been sick twelve years. The girl is twelve years old. Both are called daughter. Both are unclean by the law, one bleeding, one dead, and Jesus touches both. And the interruption that looked like it cost the girl her life turns out to be part of the same healing.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice who interrupts you. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day or two. Who stopped you when you were on your way somewhere? A child with a question. A coworker at your desk. A text from someone who needed to talk. Pick one. What did they actually need? If you pray, you can hold that person before God, and ask to see the next interruption differently. If you don't, just picture yourself stopping for them, the way Jesus stopped. The bell holds the time.
The story inside the story. Mark's sandwich: a bleeding woman healed in the middle of the story of Jairus's daughter. Two daughters, one healing. Today's word.
screen: `THE STORY INSIDE THE STORY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: interruptions are the ministry. Today, when someone stops you on your way to the important thing, consider that they might be the important thing. Day two hundred five.

206.title: The carpenter (Mark 6:1–6)
206.hook: at home they say isn't this the carpenter, and he could do few miracles there
206.howItsDone: Catholics honor Jesus's years of ordinary work in Nazareth, especially on the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker on May 1, and many offer their daily work as a prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the story inside the story: two daughters, one healing. Your line was interruptions are the ministry. Who stopped you, and did you stop? Today Jesus goes home. Day two hundred six.

Have you ever gone back to your hometown after you've changed? You walk into the old kitchen, and within ten minutes you're fourteen again. Your aunt still calls you by your childhood nickname. Somebody brings up the thing you broke in fifth grade. Nobody there has seen who you've become. They only see who you were. Jesus has been teaching, healing and calming storms around the lake. Crowds follow him everywhere. And then he goes home to Nazareth, the village where everybody knows his mother. Today: the carpenter.
screen: `BACK IN THE OLD KITCHEN.` → `FOURTEEN AGAIN.` → `JESUS GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the question. On the sabbath he teaches in the synagogue, and people are astonished. Where did he get all this? What's this wisdom? And then the astonishment curdles. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary". They list his brothers by name, and say his sisters are right here with us. And they were scandalized, Mark says: they stumbled over him. Second, the word carpenter. Mark's Greek is tekton, a builder, a craftsman who might work in wood or stone. Mark is the only gospel that calls Jesus himself a carpenter; Matthew says the carpenter's son. So for most of his life, Jesus worked with his hands. He knew splinters and calluses and customers who didn't pay on time. Catholics honor that work: on May first they keep the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker. And notice son of Mary. People were usually named by their father. Some scholars wonder whether it hints at gossip about his birth; others think it simply means Joseph had died. The text doesn't say. Third, the proverb. Jesus answers: "A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and in his own house, and among his own kindred." Fourth, the startling line. "And he could not do any miracles there, only that he cured a few that were sick, laying his hands upon them." Could not. Mark doesn't soften it. And he wondered at their unbelief. The people who knew him best were the ones who couldn't see him. Familiar had made them blind.
screen: `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` · `TEKTON: A BUILDER, HANDS AND CALLUSES.` · `A PROPHET IN HIS OWN COUNTRY.` · `HE COULD NOT DO MIRACLES THERE.` · then, large: `AND HE WONDERED BECAUSE OF THEIR UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see someone familiar freshly. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you see every day and hardly notice anymore: a parent, a partner, a roommate, a coworker, a sibling. Now picture them as a stranger would, meeting them for the first time. What's good in them that you've stopped seeing? What have they become that you haven't caught up with? If you pray, you can give thanks for them, as if they were new. The bell holds the time.
The carpenter. What his hometown called Jesus, a builder who worked with his hands, and the label that kept them from seeing him. Today's word.
Your line: familiar can blind. Today, ask one person close to you a question you've never asked, and listen to the answer as if you'd just met. Day two hundred six.

207.title: Two by two (Mark 6:7–29)
207.hook: the twelve go out with a staff and no bread; John the Baptist is killed at a party
207.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Passion of Saint John the Baptist on August 29, and the Church's missionaries and religious orders have long taken the sending of the twelve as a model of simple living; the sick receive the sacrament of anointing with blessed oil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the carpenter, and a hometown that couldn't see him. Your line was familiar can blind. Who did you see freshly? Today, the twelve are sent out, and there's a dark story in the middle. Day two hundred seven.

Think about the last time you packed for a trip. The extra charger, just in case. The spare sweater. Snacks. A backup plan for the backup plan. Most of us pack for every possible thing that could go wrong. Now imagine being sent on a journey with instructions to pack nothing. No bag. No food. No money. One walking stick and the sandals on your feet. That's how Jesus sends out the twelve apostles for the first time. And while they're out on the road, Mark tells us what happened to the man who went before them all. Today: two by two.
screen: `PACKING FOR EVERYTHING.` → `SENT WITH NOTHING.` → `AND A STORY IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: First, two by two. Jesus calls the twelve and begins to send them out in pairs. Mark doesn't say why. Jewish law said a matter was confirmed by two witnesses, and anyone who's traveled knows the simpler reason: nobody should walk alone. Second, the packing list. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he commanded them that they should take nothing for the way, but a staff only; no scrip, no bread, nor money in their purse". A scrip is a traveler's bag. Sandals, yes; two coats, no. Stay in whatever house takes you in. If a town won't hear you, shake the dust off your feet and move on. They go, and they preach that people should repent, and they anoint many sick people with oil and heal them. Catholics see in that anointing a first glimpse of the sacrament of the anointing of the sick. Third, the story in the middle. While the twelve are out, Mark cuts away, another sandwich, to King Herod. John the Baptist had told Herod he had no right to marry his brother's wife, Herodias, and Herod had him locked up. Herod feared John, and liked to listen to him, even though it troubled him. Then at Herod's birthday party, the daughter of Herodias dances, and the king, pleased and showing off for his guests, swears to give her anything. Her mother tells her what to ask for: John's head on a dish. Herod is sorry, but he won't break his oath in front of his guests. John is beheaded in prison. His disciples come and bury him. Fourth, why here? Mark puts the cost of the mission right in the middle of the mission. The ones sent out with nothing need to know how the messenger before them ended.
screen: `SENT IN PAIRS.` · `A STAFF ONLY, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.` · `OIL FOR THE SICK.` · `JOHN'S DEATH AT A PARTY.` · then, large: `TAKE NOTHING FOR THE WAY, BUT A STAFF ONLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: travel light today. Settle, and breathe. Picture everything you're carrying into today, not in your bag, in your head: the backup plans, the worst-case scenarios, the grudge from yesterday. Pick one thing to leave behind. Imagine setting it down by the door. If you pray, you can trust God with it, the way the twelve had to trust strangers for their bread. If you don't, just practice walking out without it, for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Two by two. How Jesus sent out the twelve: in pairs, with a staff and nothing else, while John the Baptist paid for his message with his life. Today's word.
Your line: take nothing for the way. Today, go somewhere with less than usual, fewer things in your pockets or fewer plans in your head, and see what you're given. Day two hundred seven.

208.title: Come apart and rest (Mark 6:30–44)
208.hook: come apart into a desert place, and rest a little, then the crowds, then the loaves
208.howItsDone: Catholics hear the feeding of the five thousand as a sign pointing to the Eucharist, and many make retreats, days apart for prayer and rest, taking this passage as their invitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two by two: the twelve sent out with nothing. Your line was take nothing for the way. What did you leave behind? Today they come back, tired. Day two hundred eight.

You know the feeling after a big stretch of work. Exams done, the shift over, the move finished, the guests gone. You come home buzzing and exhausted, with a hundred stories to tell and no energy to tell them. The twelve come back from their first mission just like that. They crowd around Jesus to report everything they did and taught. And it's so busy, Mark says, with people coming and going, that they don't even have time to eat. And Jesus says one of the kindest sentences in the gospel. Today: come apart and rest.
screen: `BACK FROM A BIG STRETCH.` → `NO TIME EVEN TO EAT.` → `ONE OF THE KINDEST SENTENCES.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the Douay-Rheims: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little. For there were many coming and going: and they had not so much as time to eat." Apart means away, by yourselves. Jesus sees tired people and prescribes rest before anything else. It's an invitation that comes from him, not a reward they've earned. Second, the crowd. They get in a boat to find a quiet place, but people see them go and run around the shore on foot, and get there first. The rest is interrupted. And Jesus, seeing the crowd, has compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. So he teaches them. Third, the loaves. It gets late. The disciples say, send them away to buy food. Jesus says: you give them something to eat. They have five loaves and two fish. He has the people sit down in groups on the green grass. Then he takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives them to the disciples to hand out. Everyone eats and is filled, and they gather up twelve baskets of leftovers. Five thousand men were fed. Fourth, those four verbs. Took, blessed, broke, gave. Catholics hear them again at every Mass, in the words over the bread at the Last Supper. So this meal in the desert points forward to the Eucharist. And it starts from an unfinished rest. The rest didn't fail. It was the beginning. Jesus never takes back the invitation: come apart, and rest a little.
screen: `COME APART: AWAY, BY YOURSELVES.` · `SHEEP WITHOUT A SHEPHERD.` · `FIVE LOAVES, TWO FISH.` · `TOOK, BLESSED, BROKE, GAVE.` · then, large: `COME APART INTO A DESERT PLACE, AND REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a real break, right now. Settle, and breathe. This is your desert place. No one is coming or going for two minutes. Let your eyes close or soften. Notice how tired you actually are, without judging it. If you pray, you can hear the invitation as if it were spoken to you: come apart, and rest a little. If you don't, just rest a little, the way you'd tell a tired friend to. The bell holds the time.
Come apart and rest. Jesus's invitation to his tired friends, before the crowds and before the loaves. Today's word.
Your line: rest a little. Today, take one real break, away from the coming and going, and eat something sitting down. Day two hundred eight.

209.title: It is I, fear not (Mark 6:45–56)
209.hook: he walks on the sea and sees them toiling in rowing
209.howItsDone: Catholics hear the walking on the water in the weekday Mass readings of the Christmas season, and many pray 'it is I, fear not' in times of fear; the phrase 'be not afraid' became a watchword of Pope John Paul II.

segments.voice: Yesterday, come apart and rest, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was rest a little. Did you sit down to eat? Tonight the disciples are back on the lake, without him. Day two hundred nine.

Three in the morning. You're pulling at something that won't move. A deadline. A sick child's fever. A relationship that keeps drifting backward no matter how hard you work at it. Your arms ache and you're not getting anywhere, and you're pretty sure no one sees. That's where the disciples are tonight. Right after the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus sends them across the lake by boat while he stays behind to pray. The wind turns against them. They row for hours and get nowhere. Today: it is I.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `PULLING AND GETTING NOWHERE.` → `NO ONE SEES.`

segments.voice: First, he sees. Jesus is on the mountain, praying, and from there he sees them. In the King James: "And he saw them toiling in rowing; for the wind was contrary unto them." They think they're alone out there. They aren't. Second, he comes. In the fourth watch of the night, somewhere between three and six in the morning, he comes to them walking on the sea. And then Mark adds a strange line: he would have passed by them. Why pass by? Scholars point to the Hebrew Bible, where God passes by Moses on the mountain, and passes by Elijah at the cave. Passing by is how God shows himself. Third, the word. The disciples see him and think it's a ghost. They scream. And straightaway he speaks. In the Douay-Rheims: "Have a good heart, it is I, fear ye not." In Mark's Greek, it is I is ego eimi, which can also be heard as I am. Those are the words God speaks to Moses at the burning bush: I am who am. So the same words mean two things at once: it's me, your friend, don't be afraid; and, I am. Fourth, the boat. He climbs in, and the wind drops. And Mark says they were astonished, because they hadn't understood about the loaves; their hearts were hardened. Mark's disciples still don't get it, and he keeps telling us so. Then they land, and people rush the sick to him on mats, begging just to touch the hem of his cloak, and all who touch it are healed. Only Matthew tells of Peter walking on the water. Mark keeps his eyes on the rowers.
screen: `HE SAW THEM TOILING IN ROWING.` · `HE WOULD HAVE PASSED BY.` · `EGO EIMI: IT IS I, I AM.` · `THE WIND DROPS; THEY STILL DON'T SEE.` · then, large: `HAVE A GOOD HEART, IT IS I, FEAR YE NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name where you're rowing hard. Settle, and breathe. Picture a small boat at night, and put yourself at the oars. What are you pulling against right now? A task, a person, an illness, a fear. Name it plainly. Notice how tired your arms are. If you pray, you can hear the words spoken into that boat: have a good heart, it is I, fear not. If you don't, simply let your arms rest for two minutes, and let the wind blow. The bell holds the time.
It is I. What Jesus says on the water to his terrified friends: in Greek, ego eimi, it's me, and I am. Today's word.
Your line: it is I. Today, when you're straining at the oars and sure nobody sees, remember the rowers weren't as alone as they thought. Day two hundred nine.

210.title: From the heart (Mark 7:1–23)
210.hook: it's what comes out of the heart that makes unclean
210.howItsDone: Catholics hear this gospel at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and many make a daily examination of conscience, reviewing their words and actions and the heart behind them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, it is I: Jesus on the water, and rowers who weren't alone. Your line was it is I. Where were you rowing hard? Today, an argument about washing hands. Day two hundred ten.

Think about the outside of your life for a second. The clean kitchen when guests come over. The polished profile picture. The right thing said at the right moment. Most of us are pretty good at the outside. Now think about the stuff that comes out of us when nobody's performing. The comment under your breath in traffic. The text you send when you're angry. What you say about someone once they've left the room. In today's reading, an argument about clean hands turns into a teaching about exactly that. Today: from the heart.
screen: `THE CLEAN KITCHEN FOR GUESTS.` → `THE COMMENT UNDER YOUR BREATH.` → `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT HANDS.`

segments.voice: First, the washing. Some Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem and notice that some of Jesus's disciples eat bread without washing their hands in the ritual way. Mark stops to explain for readers who weren't Jewish: the Pharisees, following the tradition of the elders, washed their hands before eating, and washed cups and pots too. This wasn't about germs. Many scholars explain it as a practice of holiness, bringing something of the Temple's purity to an ordinary table. Many observant Jews still wash their hands with a blessing before eating bread today. Second, the challenge. Jesus answers with the prophet Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." He gives an example: a man who declares his money set aside for God, corban, so it can't be used to support his aging parents. The rule is kept; the parents go hungry. Third, the saying. Then he calls the crowd and says it plainly: "There is nothing from without a man that entering into him, can defile him. But the things which come from a man, those are they that defile a man." Later, alone with the disciples, he explains: "For from within out of the heart of men proceed evil thoughts", and he lists them: theft, murder, greed, deceit, envy, slander, pride. Fourth, how this is read. Many translations read Mark as adding that in saying this, Jesus made all foods clean, and Christians came to eat any food. Observant Jews continue to keep the food laws as God's commandments, and hear this debate as one among teachers. Catholics hear its center clearly: God looks at the heart. What makes a life holy or unholy starts on the inside.
screen: `A TRADITION OF CLEAN HANDS.` · `LIPS NEAR, HEART FAR.` · `NOTHING FROM WITHOUT CAN DEFILE.` · `WHAT COMES OUT OF THE HEART.` · then, large: `THEIR HEART IS FAR FROM ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch your words. Settle, and breathe. Think back over yesterday. What came out of you? Not what you planned to say, what actually came out. A kind word. A sharp one. Something about someone behind their back. Don't argue with yourself; just look. Then look underneath: what was in your heart when it came out? Tired? Hurt? Afraid? If you pray, you can offer your heart to God as it is, and ask for a clean one. If you don't, just notice. The bell holds the time.
From the heart. Jesus's teaching that what makes a person unclean isn't what goes in, but what comes out of the heart. Today's word.

Your line: out of the heart. This week: Legion sent home, two daughters healed, the carpenter at home, the twelve sent out, rest, the rowers, and now the heart. Today, for one hour, listen to every word you say, and hear where it came from. Day two hundred ten.
